analysis.one_liner: Holds police accountable for misconduct, limits qualified immunity, bans chokeholds and no-knock warrants in drug cases.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 2020 with 36 cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote in the Senate Judiciary Committee and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change how police officers are held accountable when they injure or kill someone. It would make it easier to convict officers of federal civil rights violations, limit the "qualified immunity" legal shield that often gets civil lawsuits against officers thrown out, create a public national registry of police misconduct, ban federal racial profiling, require officers to wear body cameras, and cut off federal grant money to states that allow chokeholds, no-knock warrants in drug cases, or fail to report use-of-force data. It also makes lynching a federal crime. After being introduced, it was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which took no action on it before the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who are victims of police misconduct and their families: the bill would let more civil lawsuits reach a jury by limiting qualified immunity, make it easier to prosecute officers in federal court, and give DOJ subpoena power in investigations of departments with patterns of discrimination. Communities subject to stops and searches would gain enforceable anti-profiling rules and public use-of-force data, and states would face a choice between banning chokeholds and no-knock warrants in drug cases or losing federal police grants.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Victims of police misconduct and their families

how_it_helps.text: Lowers the criminal intent standard for convicting a law enforcement officer of a federal civil rights violation from "willfully" to "knowingly or with reckless disregard," making federal prosecutions easier to win.

Removes qualified immunity as a defense in civil suits against local law enforcement officers and state correctional officers, including when the constitutional right was not clearly established at the time.
Authorizes the Department of Justice to issue subpoenas in investigations of police departments for a pattern or practice of discrimination or excessive force.
Creates a National Police Misconduct Registry, open to the public, compiling complaints, discipline records, terminations, and lawsuits and settlements against officers.

Establishes a framework to prohibit racial profiling at the federal, state, and local levels, and requires federal, state, and local agencies to report data on stops, searches, and use of force, broken down by race, ethnicity, age, and gender.

Conditions federal Byrne and COPS grant funds on states banning chokeholds and carotid holds, banning no-knock warrants in drug cases, adopting a duty to intervene, and reporting use-of-force data; makes a chokehold itself a punishable civil rights violation.
Requires federal uniformed officers to wear body cameras and requires in-car video, and restricts facial recognition use on footage.
Makes lynching a federal crime under the Justice for Victims of Lynching Act title.

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement officers and their agencies: individual officers would lose the qualified immunity shield in personal civil lawsuits and face a lower federal conviction standard; police unions would see members' misconduct records made public in a national registry; state and local governments would have to change policies, collect and report data, and fund body cameras and accreditation, or lose federal grant money.
analysis.who_pays_short: Police unions, officers, and local agencies

drawbacks.text: Removing qualified immunity and lowering the intent standard exposes individual officers to personal civil liability and federal prosecution under a "knowing or reckless" standard; police groups have argued this would drive up liability costs, chill aggressive but lawful policing, and make recruiting harder.

The bill works mainly by conditioning federal grant money: states that do not ban chokeholds, ban no-knock warrants in drug cases, or meet reporting and certification requirements lose Byrne and COPS funds, which shifts costs onto state and local budgets and gives the Attorney General wide discretion to withhold or reallocate funds.

Compliance costs fall on local governments: agencies must build use-of-force reporting systems, public complaint systems, audits, and accreditation programs, and smaller departments get grants only to help them comply.

The misconduct registry publishes complaints and discipline records for every officer, raising privacy and fairness concerns for officers who are cleared or face unsubstantiated complaints, since even exonerated and unfounded complaints are compiled.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefits—civil suits that can actually reach a jury, a public misconduct registry, enforceable anti-profiling rules, and bans on chokeholds and drug-case no-knock warrants—address failures that repeatedly appear in cases where officers faced no consequences. The main costs are real but secondary: higher liability and compliance costs for departments and less control for states over their own police, enforced through grant conditions. On balance the bill's design is conventional for policing reform—most of its force comes from federal money, which is also its biggest weakness, since a future administration could simply decline to enforce the conditions.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Judiciary Committee never held a hearing or vote on it, and the bill died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the Justice in Policing Act of 2020 in the Senate on June 8, 2020, joined by 36 cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.
All 36 cosponsors were Democrats plus one independent; no Republican cosponsored the Senate bill.

The bill would have lowered the intent standard for federal civil rights prosecutions of officers, limited qualified immunity in civil suits, created a public National Police Misconduct Registry, prohibited racial profiling, required use-of-force and body-camera mandates, and conditioned federal police grants on banning chokeholds and drug-case no-knock warrants.
The action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action after the June 8 referral, and the 116th Congress ended January 3, 2021 with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Police unions and rank-and-file officers kept qualified immunity and existing use-of-force practices, since no misconduct registry, profiling ban, or liability change was enacted. State and local agencies also kept their federal grant money without new conditions.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police unions and officers who kept qualified immunity

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Justice in Policing Act of 2020 in the Senate on June 8, 2020.

for.name: Sen. Kamala Harris and Sen. Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced, with Schumer as his party's leader in the Senate.

for.name: 36 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Democrat plus one independent, none Republican.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee (Chair Lindsey Graham, R-SC)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on June 8, 2020 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it during the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; it never received a vote, and no Republican senator supported it.

against.name: Fraternal Order of Police and police unions
against.what_they_did: Opposed the accountability provisions of the Justice in Policing Act, particularly limits on qualified immunity and the lower criminal intent standard.

sides.party_line_note: All 36 Senate cosponsors were Democrats plus one independent, with no Republican support, and the bill never came to a vote, so the partisan split is measured by sponsorship rather than a roll call.

industries.industry: Police unions and rank-and-file law enforcement officers
industries.note: The bill would strip qualified immunity as a defense in civil suits against officers, lower the intent standard for federal civil rights convictions, and publish each officer's complaints, discipline, and lawsuit history in a public national registry. Its interest in blocking the bill ran against the accountability the public provisions sought.

industries.industry: State and local law enforcement agencies
industries.note: Departments would face mandatory use-of-force reporting, public complaint systems, accreditation standards, and body camera requirements, and states could lose Byrne and COPS grant money for allowing chokeholds or drug-case no-knock warrants. Some money flows to them through compliance and training grants, but the binding conditions are the compliance costs.

industries.industry: Police equipment and records vendors (body cameras, data systems)
industries.note: The bill mandates body cameras for federal officers and funds data collection, complaint systems, and accreditation, creating government purchases of recording and records technology.
